subject: general
question: An alloy contains tin and copper in the ratio 5:3. A second alloy contains tin and copper in the ratio 3:1. What quantity of the first alloy must be mixed with 20 kg of the second alloy to produce a new alloy with tin and copper in the ratio 4:2?
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Using the Alligation rule directly on the fraction of Tin in the alloys:

Fraction of Tin: Alloy 1 = 5/8, Alloy 2 = 3/4, Mixture = 4/6 = 2/3

Ratio of quantities = (3/4 − 2/3) : (2/3 − 5/8) = 1/12 : 1/24 = 2 : 1

Given 1 part (Alloy 2) corresponds to 20 kg.

So, 2 parts (Alloy 1) = 2 × 20 = 40 kg.

**∴ The correct answer is 40 kg.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Ratio of Tin to Copper in Alloy 1 = 5 : 3

Ratio of Tin to Copper in Alloy 2 = 3 : 1

Target Ratio of Tin to Copper in New Alloy = 4 : 2 = 2 : 1

Quantity of Alloy 2 = 20 kg

**Formula Used:**

Alligation method applied to fractions of a single component (Tin) in the mixtures.

 
• 
• 
• 
• Alloy 1 (5/8) Alloy 2 (3/4) Mix (2/3) 1/12 1/24 Ratio = 1/12 : 1/24 = 2 : 1 

**Calculations:**

⇒ Fraction of Tin in Alloy 1 = 5 ÷ (5 + 3) = 5/8

⇒ Fraction of Tin in Alloy 2 = 3 ÷ (3 + 1) = 3/4

⇒ Fraction of Tin in New Alloy = 4 ÷ (4 + 2) = 4/6 = 2/3

Applying the rule of alligation to find the required ratio of quantities:

⇒ Ratio of Alloy 1 to Alloy 2 = (3/4 − 2/3) : (2/3 − 5/8)

⇒ Ratio = (9/12 − 8/12) : (16/24 − 15/24)

⇒ Ratio = 1/12 : 1/24

⇒ Required Ratio = 2 : 1

We are given that the quantity of Alloy 2 used is 20 kg (which represents 1 unit in the ratio):

⇒ Quantity of Alloy 1 = 2 × 20 kg

⇒ Quantity of Alloy 1 = 40 kg

**∴ The correct answer is 40 kg.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Alligation Method

It is a rule used to quickly find the ratio in which two or more ingredients must be mixed to produce a specific desired average or concentration. It can be applied on percentages, prices, and component fractions.

Replacement Method

If a container holds x units of pure liquid and y units are taken out and replaced by water n times, the remaining quantity of pure liquid is given by x × (1 − y/x)ⁿ.

Multiple Mixtures

When combining multiple mixtures containing differing ratios of the same components, always evaluate the quantities by converting the component ratios into absolute fractional parts out of the whole before combining them.
